To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the downstream development unit is able, in equilibrium, to control ex interim the amount of licencing fees, and (ii) such interim inefficient control is renegotiation proof.

1) The downstream development unit's ability to prevent the formation of financial coalitions between upstream research unit and outside investors, at the ex interim licensing stage, can give the downstream unit control rights that allow her to extract a larger share of the interim innovation's value, 2) The downstream unit is more likely to have such control rights when the ex interim value of the interim innovation is lower, and when the ex interim financial constraint of the upstream research unit is more likely, to bind,

(i) the downstream development unit can control the upstream research unit by restricting its ability to form financial coalitions at an ex interim stage; (ii) the control rights are renegotiation-proof; (iii) the control rights can be used to induce the research unit to exert more effort ex ante.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of control rights in corporate venturing and bankruptcy regimes.
the optimal allocation of interim control rights in the development and licensing of innovative knowledge, in the presence of ex interim financial constraints.
the role of control rights in facilitating efficient innovation and the role of bankruptcy regimes in shaping the optimal control rights.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the control rights that arise in the context of the licensing of interim innovations are a function of the value of the interim innovation and the relative bargaining power of the two units.

the downstream development unit is able and willing to exert interim control rights, and that such control rights can be efficient, but only if the downstream unit is able to credibly commit to the interim mode of licensing.
the control rights of the development unit are not only consistent with but actually serve the interests of the research unit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the control rights of the development unit are not a substitute for the innovator's property rights, but rather an addition to them.

, in the context of corporate venturing, the control rights that arise from the downstream development unit's ability to prevent financial coalitions between the upstream research unit and third parties, are a key mechanism for inducing more research effort ex ante, and that such interim inefficient rights may not be renegotiation proof in the context of bankruptcy.
the inalienability constraint on initial intellectual property rights is a key determinant of the optimal structure of control rights over interim innovations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the presence of a downstream unit's ability to control the mode of licensing at the ex interim phase of bargaining, the upstream unit's ability to form coalitions at the interim phase of bargaining is limited.

control rights over intellectual property are a natural and efficient response to the inalienability and indivisibility of initial intellectual property rights, and that such control rights can arise endogenously in equilibrium.

the ex interim bargaining over the structure of control rights can be used as a tool to align the interests of the research unit with that of the downstream development unit, and to incentivise the former to exert more effort ex ante.
